options: fopen returns NULL if the file does not exist or cannot be opened; without checking, subsequent operations on f cause undefined behavior
fopen never fails; the check is unnecessary
Compiler error if fopen is not checked
NULL indicates success; non-NULL indicates failure
explanation: fopen returns NULL on failure; operations like fread/fprintf on a NULL FILE* are undefined behavior.

options: hello (mode w truncates the file; fprintf writes the new content)
Compiler error: mode w cannot write
Garbage or old data (w mode does not actually write)
Nothing (w mode leaves the file empty)
explanation: Mode w opens for writing and truncates the file; fprintf writes the content; close flushes buffers.

options: The number of bytes successfully read (0 to 10, or EOF if end of file reached)
The total size of the buffer (always 10)
The file size
Compiler error: fread returns void
explanation: fread returns the number of items actually read; if fewer than 10 bytes are available, n is less than 10.

options: Moves the file position 10 bytes from the start; fgetc reads the character at that position
Reads 10 characters
Seeks backward 10 bytes
Compiler error: fseek requires a specific mode
explanation: fseek moves the file pointer; SEEK_SET is absolute from the start, SEEK_CUR is relative, SEEK_END is from the end.

options: Mode a appends to the end; mode w truncates and overwrites
Mode a and w are identical
Mode a is faster than mode w
Mode w is for binary files; mode a is for text
explanation: Mode a opens for appending; writes go to the end. Mode w truncates the existing file.

options: fread reads from the current position (after fprintf's write); to read the modified data, fseek to the beginning or flush the buffer
Mode r+ is read-only; writing is not allowed
fprintf and fread cannot be mixed
Compiler error: mode r+ is invalid
explanation: Interleaving reads and writes requires careful buffer management; fflush or fseek ensures data is written before reading.

options: Binary mode prevents text-mode line-ending conversions (\r\n on Windows); text mode may alter data
Binary mode is faster
Binary mode allows only unsigned data types
Text mode and binary mode are identical on most systems
explanation: On systems like Windows, text mode converts line endings; binary mode reads/writes exactly what is in the file.

options: Undefined behavior / data loss: buffers may not be flushed; fclose ensures all buffered data is written
The data is automatically saved even without fclose
Only the second fprintf is written; the first is lost
Compiler error: fclose is missing
explanation: fclose flushes and closes the file; omitting it may leave data in buffers, causing data loss or corruption.

options: fgets takes a size parameter (100) to prevent buffer overflow; gets has no bounds check
gets and fgets are equivalent; naming differs
fgets is deprecated; scanf should be used instead
fgets can only read text files; gets reads any file
explanation: gets is deprecated because it cannot prevent buffer overflow; fgets(buffer, 100, f) ensures at most 99 chars plus \0.

options: feof returns true only after a read attempt reaches EOF; calling it before a failed read is a common mistake
feof can be called anytime to predict EOF
feof is required before every read
Compiler error: feof is not a standard function
explanation: feof is a post-condition check; the typical pattern is to check fread's return value, not feof itself.
